doc.title: Oscar Peterson interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Teaching young players and what hurts jazz today
summary: Peterson tells students at York University to listen to the greats and complains that money and agents distract them.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: He was, yes. I’m thankful that I was fortunate enough to have been reared in that era, even though I was a bystander, I was a listener at the outset of it, and was fortunate enough to be able to hear all of these greats and learn from them. And that’s the thing that I tell, I teach at York University in Toronto, and I tell the young players, you know they come to me with problems, I say, “go down to the record library and get this album by Johnny Hodges or this album by Ben Webster, or this album by Coleman Hawkins, or Roy Eldridge, or Dizzy, and listen to it,” you know. Because that’s the whole thing I think that is a detriment to the growth of jazz today, is that business, money certainly, agents and everything have intervened to the point where the youngsters heads are filled with things other than their musical things. They’re filled with how many people did we get in this auditorium, how many albums can you sell, how many dates can you do in a year, and this sort of thing.
That’s right. And the thing is, you have to first settle, as I said, you have to first settle your thing with that instrument.
Negotiate with that instrument every night. I have to negotiate with mine. Every single performance I have to negotiate, say now how we going to do this tonight?
